fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so here's the thing. There are some things that evolution encodes that are easy to understand. Like, if you eat food, it tastes good. If you hurt yourself, it feels bad. Those are low-level sensory signals, and it's not hard to imagine how a genome could wire those up. There's some receptor, some chemical, some reward, and you can see how it's done.

But then there are desires that are very different. Like, people care a lot about what other people think of them. They care about their social standing. They care about being respected, about not being embarrassed in front of a group. And the thing is, that's a very high-level concept. To even have that desire, you need to have some representation of other people, of their minds, of the society around you, of what counts as status in that society. Those are all very abstract things that live somewhere deep inside the representations the brain learns over time.

And yet, evolution found a way to hardwire a desire about them. And it does it very robustly. It's not something that you can easily train away or reason away. Children have it very early on. It shows up in basically every human. So somehow the hardware was able to say, "whatever this high-level thing is that you'll learn later, I want you to care about it." And I don't know how that's done. It's not obvious how a relatively simple genetic specification can reach into a learned world model and point at the right abstraction.

I think about this because it's actually related to the question of value functions and what you want an AI to care about. When we train models, we have reward signals, and the easy ones are easy, just like the low-level ones are easy for evolution. But if you want something to robustly care about some very high-level, abstract thing, then evolution is an existence proof that it's possible. We just don't know the mechanism. And when you see an existence proof like that without knowing the mechanism, that's exactly the kind of thing I'd call mysterious.

r001.rationale: It describes social standing and respect as abstract outcomes that require learned representations of other people and society, then asks how evolution can hardwire a desire that points to them.

r002.rationale: It says the brain learns representations of social concepts, but does not explain that acquiring sophisticated desires during life is understandable because an intelligent brain can learn them.

opus-5.5.text:
What I find mysterious is this. When I think about how evolution gives us our desires, the low-level ones seem quite understandable. Take the desire for food that smells good. A smell is a chemical, and you can imagine evolution saying: when this chemical is detected, produce a reward. The mapping is simple and hardcoded. Fine.

But we also have desires that are much more abstract. People care a great deal about how they're seen by others, about their standing in a group, about whether they're being treated fairly, about being respected. These desires are very strong, and they seem to have been built in by evolution. Our ancestors needed them to survive in social groups.

Here's the puzzle. To even know whether your social standing is going up or down, your brain has to do an enormous amount of processing. It has to understand other people, model what they think, interpret subtle signals. That's a high-level representation, assembled out of a huge amount of learned computation. And yet evolution has somehow managed to say: "Care about *that*." How do you point the reward at something so abstract, when the thing you're pointing at is itself the product of learning?

It isn't like hooking a reward up to a sensor. And evolution did it with a fairly limited genome, and apparently quite quickly in evolutionary terms.

One idea I've considered is that it's done by location: the relevant computation reliably happens in a particular brain region, and evolution simply wires a reward to "whatever happens over there." But that doesn't really hold up. There are cases where people lose large parts of their brain, even half of it, especially when young, and the functions relocate. People born blind have their visual cortex repurposed for other things. So the brain's layout is not that fixed, yet these social desires still appear quite reliably.

So I don't have a good answer. I think it's a genuinely interesting open question. And I suspect that if we understood how evolution does this, it would tell us something important about how to give AI systems robust, high-level values that point at the right abstract things.

r001.rationale: The response says social standing must be inferred by modeling others and interpreting subtle signals, then frames the puzzle as how evolution can direct reward toward that abstract outcome.

r002.rationale: It describes the computation for assessing social standing as learned, but does not explain that sophisticated desires acquired during life are understandable because an intelligent brain can learn them.

fable-5.text:
Because when you think about it, it's not clear how it could be done at all. Consider the desires that are easy to explain. Evolution wants you to eat, so it makes food smell good, taste good. That's a low-level signal. The smell of food is something you can detect with a sensor that's easy to hardwire, so you can imagine how the genome specifies it: here is a chemical, when you detect it, that's good, seek it out. Fine.

But now consider something like caring about what other people think of you. Caring about your social standing, your place in the hierarchy, whether your peers respect you. People care about this intensely — it's one of the strongest desires people have, and it shows up reliably in essentially every human being. But "social standing" is not a chemical. It's not a low-level sensory signal. It's a very high-level, abstract concept that the brain only comes to represent after a great deal of learning — learning about other people, about minds, about how they see you. The neurons that represent it, wherever they are, are presumably arranged somewhat differently in every person, because they're the product of each person's experience.

So the puzzle is: how does the genome point at that? The genome is this fairly compact description, and somehow it says, "when the brain — after years of learning — develops the concept of other people's opinion of you, attach a strong desire to it." It's reaching into a representation that doesn't exist yet at birth, that will be learned, and it somehow knows where to find it, and it does so robustly, across billions of people. I don't know how it's done. Maybe there's some trick, some indirect signal that bootstraps it. But I find it genuinely mysterious, and I think it's relevant for AI, because it suggests it is possible to specify desires about high-level learned concepts in a way that's robust — evolution did it somehow — and we don't currently know how to do that.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the puzzle: social standing is an abstract outcome learned by the brain rather than directly sensed, yet evolution appears to make people strongly desire it.

r002.rationale: It says the brain learns the concept of social standing, but does not explain that acquiring sophisticated desires during life is understandable because an intelligent brain can learn them.

opus-5.text:
Here's the thing that puzzles me. Some drives are easy to imagine being encoded. Hunger, pain, temperature — there's a sensor, there's a chemical signal, you can see how a small amount of DNA could wire up something that says "this signal, bad." That doesn't require any concepts.

But consider something like the desire to be respected by your peers, or the fact that you love your children, or that you feel embarrassed. To want to be respected, you need to have a representation of other people, a representation of their attitude toward you, and a representation of yourself as seen by them. Those are very high-level, abstract concepts, and crucially, the genome doesn't build them. They're learned. Your cortex figures them out from experience.

So evolution has to do something that, from a machine learning perspective, seems quite difficult. It has to say: whatever representation your brain ends up learning for "the people around me and what they think of me" — attach a strong drive to that. It's specifying a reward function over learned latent variables of a network it didn't train and couldn't inspect. In ML we find this hard. It's easy to reward a game score. It's much harder to reward "be a good friend," because you'd need a classifier for that, and the classifier is itself the hard part.

And yet it works, extremely reliably, in essentially every human, and it generalizes. People feel status anxiety about things that didn't exist ten thousand years ago. The drive somehow latches onto the right concept even in a totally novel environment.

I think it's possible this tells us the learned representations are more canonical than we assume — predictable enough that evolution can reliably point at them. If so, that's interesting, and maybe encouraging. But I genuinely don't know how it's done.

r001.rationale: It identifies the puzzle as evolution attaching a drive to abstract social concepts—such as others’ opinions—that the genome does not directly build and the brain learns.

r002.rationale: It says the cortex figures out these concepts from experience, explaining how sophisticated desires can be acquired through learning during life.

sonnet-5.5.text:
What I find mysterious is the contrast with the simple desires. It's easy to see how evolution gives us a desire for good-smelling food. Smell is a chemical signal, and you can imagine a fairly direct wiring from "this molecule is present" to "go toward it." That feels like something evolution could just hardcode.

But we also care a great deal about social things. We care about being seen positively by others, about our standing, about being treated fairly, about what other people think of us. Those desires are strong, and most of us feel them very powerfully. They're also high-level. To know that you're being respected or looked down on, the brain has to do a huge amount of processing. It has to integrate a lot of information about what other people are doing, what they might be thinking, and how they're reacting to you. That isn't a raw sensory signal. It's an abstraction built up deep inside the brain.

So how does evolution say "you should care about *this*" when "this" is a complicated, learned, high-level concept? Evolution doesn't know in advance what any particular brain will represent or where. I can imagine it hardcoding something like "the neurons at this location are the ones that matter." But the brain is more flexible than that. Regions can take on different functions, and people recover in surprising ways from damage or from unusual developmental circumstances. So a fixed-location story doesn't seem to be the answer.

Somehow evolution reached into this very sophisticated, learned part of the brain and attached strong values to those concepts, and it did so reliably, across almost all humans. I don't have a good explanation for how it did that, and that's why I find it so puzzling.

r001.rationale: The response frames the puzzle as how evolution attaches strong desires to social outcomes such as respect and standing, which the brain must infer from complex information rather than directly sense.

r002.rationale: It describes social concepts as learned and says the brain processes information about others, but does not explain that acquiring sophisticated desires over a lifetime is understandable because an intelligent brain can learn them.

haiku-5.5.text:
Part of what makes it strange is how little the genome has to work with. Its information content is limited, and it has to specify a huge range of outcomes. Yet people reliably end up caring about how others see them, whether they're respected, and whether they feel shame after letting someone down. Those desires aren't simple sensory signals. They're defined in terms of concepts like "what this person thinks of me," and the brain has to construct those concepts from experience.

So how does a fixed set of genetic instructions point at something that doesn't exist until the cortex has learned a model of the world? The reward has to be specified in terms of a representation that forms after birth and differs from person to person. Evolution has to get the learning system to latch onto the right thing without a hardwired description of it.

For something like face detection or a basic sensory pattern, I can imagine a circuit that does the job. For "I want my standing in my community to be high," I don't have a good mechanism in mind. I don't think anyone has a convincing answer yet, and I'd be wary of anyone who claims to. But I think it's a real clue that the learning machinery and the reward machinery are coupled in ways we don't understand well.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the puzzle as how genetic instructions can produce desires for inferred social concepts, such as respect or standing, that the brain constructs from experience rather than directly senses.

r002.rationale: It says the brain constructs these concepts from experience, but does not explain that acquiring sophisticated desires over a lifetime is understandable because an intelligent brain can learn them.

astra-6.text:
Well, the thing that’s mysterious to me is the level of abstraction. Evolution operates on genes, and genes specify how the brain develops. So you can imagine how evolution could make you like a particular taste. You have a receptor, it detects something, and you connect that to a reward signal. There’s a fairly direct story you can tell.

But consider wanting other people to think highly of you. That’s a very complicated thing to want. You need to understand that there are other people, that they have beliefs, that some of those beliefs are about you. All of that understanding is learned. And yet evolution somehow makes you care very strongly about the result of this computation.

How does it do that? How do the genes specify a desire about a concept that the brain hasn’t even learned yet? They don’t get to directly refer to whatever neurons will eventually represent your reputation. Those representations develop through experience.

So it’s not mysterious that evolution would favor caring about social status. You can see why that would be useful. The mystery is the implementation: how you build something into the developing brain that reliably attaches motivation to such a complicated, learned concept. That’s the part I find really interesting.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes directly sensed tastes from reputation, which depends on learned representations of other people’s beliefs, and asks how genes attach motivation to that inferred concept.

r002.rationale: It says the brain learns the relevant understanding through experience, making clear that the sophisticated concept is acquired during life.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, consider the desire to be respected by other people. That seems like a very complicated thing for evolution to put into your brain. You need to understand what another person is, what they think about you, and whether that thought constitutes respect. These are sophisticated concepts that you learn as you grow up.

With hunger, you can at least imagine a relatively direct mechanism: there’s some signal about the state of your body, and your brain is wired to respond to it. But wanting other people to think highly of you—how does evolution specify that? How does your genome arrange for your motivation to attach to this particular concept, when the concept itself hasn’t been learned yet?

It can’t simply specify the whole concept in advance. And yet, across very different experiences, people reliably develop these social desires. So the mystery is the mechanism connecting something specified genetically to these very abstract representations that emerge through learning.

sol-6.text: Because these desires are so abstract. Hunger seems relatively straightforward: the body can detect a deficit and make you want food. But wanting other people to respect you requires understanding other people, their beliefs about you, and the social world you grow up in. Somehow evolution gives us a brain that learns all of that and then cares deeply about it. How genes manage to point a learning system toward something so high level is what I find mysterious.

terra-5.6.text: Because the genome is such a low-bandwidth channel, yet evolution somehow uses it to produce minds with remarkably rich, high-level social drives—love for children, attachment, loyalty, concern for what others think. It’s striking that all of that can be encoded in DNA and then reliably emerge from development and experience.

sol-5.6.text: Because the genome somehow causes the brain to care about very abstract things—status, belonging, approval, fairness—even though those concepts are learned rather than directly specified at birth. Evolution only has access to relatively low-level biological machinery, yet it manages to create motivational systems that later attach themselves to high-level representations formed through experience. How it reliably makes that connection is, to me, quite mysterious.

luna-5.6.text: What I find mysterious is that evolution is operating through very simple mechanisms—selection on genes and reproductive success—yet it produces these incredibly high-level, abstract desires. We don’t just want food or safety; we care about status, fairness, being respected, loyalty, what other people think of us, and sometimes even abstract principles that have no obvious immediate benefit to us. It’s not mysterious that social behavior would be selected for, but it is mysterious how the machinery gets organized into such rich, context-sensitive concepts and subjective motivations.

luna-6.text: What I find mysterious is how something as blind and local as evolution can produce these very abstract-seeming desires. We care about being respected, belonging to a group, having influence, being seen as competent. Evolution didn’t have a concept of respect or social standing and decide to build those into us. It just selected for behaviors that helped organisms survive and reproduce, and somehow that process gave rise to these powerful motives that feel like they’re about much more than survival.
